```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

set.seed(8105)
```

# Problem 1

The function below draws a birthday for each of `n_people` people, uniformly from 365 days with replacement, and returns `TRUE` if at least two people share a birthday.

```{r p1_function}
bday_sim = function(n_people) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)

  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}
```

Next, I run the function 10,000 times for each group size from 2 to 50 and average the results to estimate the probability of a shared birthday. For comparison, I also compute the exact probability, $1 - \prod_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{365 - k}{365}$.

```{r p1_simulation}
bday_results =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(shared = map_lgl(group_size, bday_sim)) |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(prob_shared = mean(shared)) |>
  mutate(
    prob_exact = map_dbl(group_size, \(n) 1 - prod((365 - 0:(n - 1)) / 365))
  )

first_over_half =
  bday_results |>
  filter(prob_shared > 0.5) |>
  pull(group_size) |>
  min()
```

```{r p1_plot}
bday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_shared)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = prob_exact), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability that at least two people share a birthday",
    subtitle = "Points: 10,000 simulations per group size; dashed line: exact probability",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday"
  )
```

The probability of a shared birthday rises quickly with group size and follows an S-shaped curve. With `r min(bday_results$group_size)` people it is only about `r round(bday_results$prob_shared[1] * 100, 1)`%, but it first exceeds 50% at a group size of `r first_over_half`, and by `r max(bday_results$group_size)` people it reaches about `r round(max(bday_results$prob_shared) * 100, 1)`%. This is much faster than most people expect, because the number of possible pairs grows quadratically with group size: `r first_over_half` people already form `r choose(first_over_half, 2)` pairs. The simulated estimates sit almost exactly on the exact curve, so 10,000 runs per group size are enough to estimate these probabilities well. In real life birthdays are not uniform across the year, which only makes a shared birthday slightly more likely than these results suggest.

# Problem 2

The longitudinal study data has one CSV file per participant, and each file name gives the study arm (`con` or `exp`) and the subject ID. I start with a dataframe of all file names from `list.files`, then use `purrr::map` to read each subject's data into a list column.

```{r p2_import}
study_df =
  tibble(file_name = list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$")) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(file.path("data", file_name), \(path) read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE))
  )
```

To tidy the result, I pull the arm and subject ID out of the file name, unnest the subject data, and pivot the eight weekly columns into one row per subject per week. Subject IDs restart at 01 in each arm, so I also make a `subject` variable that is unique across arms.

```{r p2_tidy}
study_tidy =
  study_df |>
  mutate(file_name = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")) |>
  separate(file_name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_", remove = FALSE) |>
  rename(subject = file_name) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    names_transform = as.integer,
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("con", "exp"), labels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  ) |>
  select(subject, arm, subject_id, week, observation)

study_tidy
```

The tidy dataset has `r nrow(study_tidy)` rows, one for each of `r n_distinct(study_tidy$subject)` subjects (`r sum(study_tidy$arm == "Control") / 8` per arm) in each of `r n_distinct(study_tidy$week)` weeks.

```{r p2_spaghetti}
arm_means =
  study_tidy |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarize(mean_obs = mean(observation), .groups = "drop")

study_tidy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, color = arm)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = subject), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = arm_means, aes(y = mean_obs), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "steelblue", "Experimental" = "darkorange")) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations for each subject, by study arm",
    subtitle = "Thin lines: individual subjects; thick lines: arm means",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```

```{r p2_arm_summary}
arm_means |>
  filter(week %in% c(1, 8)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = week, names_prefix = "week_", values_from = mean_obs) |>
  mutate(change = week_8 - week_1) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Arm", "Mean at week 1", "Mean at week 8", "Change")
  )

arm_week1 = arm_means |> filter(week == 1) |> pull(mean_obs, name = arm)
arm_week8 = arm_means |> filter(week == 8) |> pull(mean_obs, name = arm)

week8_range =
  study_tidy |>
  filter(week == 8) |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(min_obs = min(observation), max_obs = max(observation))

exp_week8_min = week8_range |> filter(arm == "Experimental") |> pull(min_obs)
con_week8_max = week8_range |> filter(arm == "Control") |> pull(max_obs)
```

The two arms start at similar values: at week 1 the mean observation is `r round(arm_week1["Control"], 2)` in the control arm and `r round(arm_week1["Experimental"], 2)` in the experimental arm, and the individual trajectories overlap a lot. Over the eight weeks, subjects in the experimental arm show a steady upward trend, while control subjects fluctuate around a roughly constant level with no clear trend. By week 8 the experimental mean has risen to `r round(arm_week8["Experimental"], 2)`, compared with `r round(arm_week8["Control"], 2)` for the control arm. At week 8 the arms no longer overlap at all: the lowest experimental subject (`r exp_week8_min`) is above the highest control subject (`r con_week8_max`). Within each arm there is a lot of week-to-week variability for individual subjects, but the difference between the arms grows over time, which suggests the experimental condition increases the outcome.


# Problem 3

This problem uses simulation to study the power of a one-sample t-test. The design is fixed at $n = 30$ and $\sigma = 5$. The function below draws one sample of size `n` from $Normal(\mu, \sigma)$, tests $H: \mu = 0$ with `t.test`, and uses `broom::tidy` to return the estimate $\hat{\mu}$ and the p-value.

```{r p3_function}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  sim_sample = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  t.test(sim_sample, mu = 0) |>
    tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
}
```

First I generate 5,000 datasets with $\mu = 0$. Here the null is true, so the rejection rate at $\alpha = 0.05$ should be close to 5%.

```{r p3_mu_zero}
sim_mu_zero =
  tibble(iter = 1:5000) |>
  mutate(test = map(iter, \(i) sim_t_test(mu = 0))) |>
  unnest(test)

sim_mu_zero |>
  summarize(
    mean_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat),
    rejection_rate = mean(p_value < 0.05)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Average estimate", "Proportion rejected"))
```

When $\mu = 0$ the null is rejected in `r round(mean(sim_mu_zero$p_value < 0.05) * 100, 1)`% of datasets, close to the nominal 5% type I error rate. Next I repeat the simulation for $\mu = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ and combine the results with the $\mu = 0$ runs.

```{r p3_simulation}
sim_results =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 1:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(test = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)) |>
  unnest(test) |>
  bind_rows(mutate(sim_mu_zero, true_mu = 0)) |>
  mutate(reject = p_value < 0.05) |>
  arrange(true_mu, iter)

sim_summary =
  sim_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject),
    avg_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat),
    avg_mu_hat_rejected = mean(mu_hat[reject])
  )

sim_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("True mean", "Power", "Average estimate (all)", "Average estimate (null rejected)")
  )
```

```{r p3_power_plot}
sim_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test by true mean",
    subtitle = "n = 30, sigma = 5, alpha = 0.05; 5,000 simulated datasets per true mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Power (proportion of nulls rejected)"
  )
```

Power increases with effect size. Because $n$ and $\sigma$ are fixed, the true mean $\mu$ sets the effect size, $\mu / \sigma$. When $\mu = 0$ the rejection rate is just the type I error rate of about 5%. Power rises steeply after that, to `r round(sim_summary$power[sim_summary$true_mu == 1] * 100, 1)`% at $\mu = 1$, `r round(sim_summary$power[sim_summary$true_mu == 2] * 100, 1)`% at $\mu = 2$, and `r round(sim_summary$power[sim_summary$true_mu == 3] * 100, 1)`% at $\mu = 3$. It then levels off near 100% for $\mu \geq 4$. Larger effects move the sampling distribution of $\hat{\mu}$ further from 0 relative to its standard error ($\sigma / \sqrt{n} \approx$ `r round(5 / sqrt(30), 2)`), so the test is more likely to detect them.

```{r p3_estimate_plot}
sim_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    avg_mu_hat:avg_mu_hat_rejected,
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "avg_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    samples = recode(
      samples,
      avg_mu_hat = "All samples",
      avg_mu_hat_rejected = "Samples where the null was rejected"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_estimate, color = samples)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average estimated mean by true mean",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: average estimate equals the true mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimate of the mean",
    color = NULL
  )
```

Across all samples, the average $\hat{\mu}$ is essentially equal to the true $\mu$ for every value, because the sample mean is an unbiased estimator. The average $\hat{\mu}$ among only the samples where the null was rejected is different. It is clearly larger than the true mean when power is low: for $\mu = 1$ it is `r round(sim_summary$avg_mu_hat_rejected[sim_summary$true_mu == 1], 2)`, and for $\mu = 2$ it is `r round(sim_summary$avg_mu_hat_rejected[sim_summary$true_mu == 2], 2)`. The gap shrinks as $\mu$ grows, and for $\mu \geq 4$ the two averages are nearly the same.

This happens because conditioning on rejection selects samples. A sample only rejects the null if $\hat{\mu}$ lands far enough from 0, about 2 standard errors (roughly `r round(qt(0.975, df = 29) * 5 / sqrt(30), 2)`). When the true effect is small, most samples fall short of this cutoff, so the samples that pass are mostly ones that overestimated $\mu$ by chance, and their average is biased upward. When power is near 100%, almost every sample is rejected, so the rejected samples are essentially all samples and their average is close to the true $\mu$. At $\mu = 0$ the rejected-sample average stays near 0 only because large positive and large negative estimates cancel out. This is why significant results from underpowered studies tend to overstate the true effect size.
